sources.title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
sources.note: Full transcript, README and meta read. Dex and Vaibhav; cards only where Dex argues or endorses. Inventory lists title only (2026-05 line), no URL.

sources.title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
sources.note: Full transcript, README and meta read. Guest Rhys Sullivan (Executor) drives most of the content; guest ideas carded as author other only where Dex adopts them. Inventory lists title only (2026-05 line).

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can context engineer the models faster than the labs can release a new model every six months
cards.claim: Dex argues that building your own context engineering and harness on top of a model beats waiting for the lab, because labs ship new models only every few months.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as an argument against the 'bitter lessoned away' claim; no numbers, a reasoning-trace example (small models with thinking off).
cards.landing: Justifies keeping a custom FixFlow outer harness (phase routine, workflows) rather than waiting for lab features.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you have like the model... and then what we might call the inner harness
cards.claim: Dex splits a coding agent into the model, an inner harness (tool definitions, implementations, what tools return, such as offloading long bash output and rejecting long reads) and an outer harness (orchestration around it).
cards.evidence_detail: Examples given: edit returns file info, long bash output auto-offloaded to a file, long reads rejected in favour of limit/offset.
cards.landing: Vocabulary for the review: FixFlow only controls the outer harness (CLAUDE.md, routine, workflows); tool-output shaping sits in the inner harness.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: If you've got a while loop that has more information than the one inside of it does, you can do better.
cards.claim: Dex endorses Vaibhav's framing that alpha comes from stacking outer loops that carry more information about the process (RPI is such a loop around the inner agent loop).
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's drawing; Dex agrees ('this is a really good picture'), cites Codex goal mode / Ralph-style orchestrators as another stacked loop. Vaibhav said RPI boosted him more than any model or harness choice.
cards.landing: Supports the phase routine and saved workflows as outer loops that carry process knowledge (phase, PR, register ids) the inner agent lacks.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't think there's a moat in it.
cards.claim: Dex says a new orchestrator layer (e.g. a goal-generating loop that fans out to goal-completing loops) is probably about a hundred lines of Python or TypeScript, so he treats such stacking as hype with no moat.
cards.evidence_detail: Reaction to a posted orchestrator built on Codex goal mode.
cards.landing: Caution against heavy investment in a bespoke multi-agent orchestration library; a saved workflow script is cheap and replaceable.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you start your context window at 50,000 tokens because there's 32,000 tokens of tools
cards.claim: Dex says Opus 4.7 in Claude Code with no customisation starts at about 50k tokens (32k tools plus 10k system prompt) before any user content.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated from memory in answer to a chat question about why Claude Code is a poor harness for 4.7; no measurement shown.
cards.landing: Context budget accounting: baseline load of tools/system prompt plus CLAUDE.md (390 lines) counts against the working window each phase.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: if you're doing a hundred turn operation, reducing your accuracy by 1% actually has like a 25% impact
cards.claim: Dex cites the compounding chart: a small per-call accuracy loss over a hundred-plus tool calls drops end-to-end success sharply, so tool shape matters in long agent runs.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex recalls Vaibhav's chart (1% per-step loss gives roughly 25% or more at 100 steps); Vaibhav adds 'real fast' at 500 calls. Arithmetic, not an experiment.
cards.landing: Argues for fewer steps and fewer unverified handoffs per phase; informs per-phase step budgets and verifier placement.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: reasonably, the tools are damn simple. There is no nested object
cards.claim: Dex says Claude Code works because its core tools (read, write, edit, bash) are simple with no nested objects, so the model has a good chance of calling them correctly.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's synthesis after the recursive-types/discriminated-unions discussion; also notes the Anthropic API did not support discriminated unions.
cards.landing: Design rule for any custom agent, skill or script interface FixFlow adds: flat, simple tool/argument shapes.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The worst harness in the world is just YOLO prompting a model.
cards.claim: Dex says a dumb model with a narrowly scoped, optimised harness can beat a strong model with a bad harness, and the spectrum runs from YOLO prompting to fully programmatic control.
cards.evidence_detail: Answer to a chat question; ties to the context engineering argument, no numbers. Vaibhav: 'depends on the delta'.
cards.landing: Supports effort/model routing: narrow, well-scoped steps let cheaper models or lower effort work; the harness does the heavy lifting.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: been experimenting a lot with 5.5 on low mode.
cards.claim: Dex reports using GPT-5.5 on low reasoning effort for already-planned work, and warns that extra-high effort can produce absurd over-testing (a thousand unit tests for a button colour change).
cards.evidence_detail: Personal usage; the over-testing story is second-hand from Ben Davis and others. He says he has not yet formed a feel for higher effort levels.
cards.landing: Effort routing: default low effort for execution of a settled plan; cap effort for verifiers to avoid over-elaboration.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude is nice for human readable plans... short and high level.
cards.claim: Dex uses Claude for plans a human will read and interact with (short, high level, human-sounding) and GPT on high/xhigh when he does not want to spend time making the model build code-base understanding first.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal model-by-task preference stated at end of episode.
cards.landing: Model-per-task routing: plan and owner-view writing on one model, deep codebase understanding on another.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: It's the velocity, not the position.
cards.claim: Dex endorses the view that durable skill is rebuilding on each new model/harness release, not mastering any one loop, so test each new model against your own case.
cards.evidence_detail: Closing exchange; Vaibhav: 'Your job is to always build the next while loop' and A/B-test each new model for customer value.
cards.landing: Argues for periodic re-evaluation of the harness (model, effort, verifier choices) rather than freezing the phase routine.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: for every one good article, there's like 10... half AI written slop of people just engagement farming
cards.claim: Dex says most harness engineering articles are AI-written engagement farming and that his job is to cut through hype and jargon, warning against copying them uncritically.
cards.evidence_detail: Opening framing, tied to an OpenAI engineer's apology for 'harness engineering hype'.
cards.landing: Source-quality caution for the review; nowhere obvious in the harness.

cards.source_title: OpenAI tells you not to build your own harness (AITW #56)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Can dumb model with good harness beat the good model with bad harness?
cards.claim: Dex treats lab-trained tool shapes as mattering mostly for tool-calling reliability: swapping to a differently trained model in the same harness degrades results, and he describes a proxy that can divert one harness's traffic to another model.
cards.evidence_detail: Claims GPT-5 in the Claude Code harness gets 'terrible' performance (Vaibhav corrects to 'slightly different'); no measurement.
cards.landing: Caution on running the same agent files or skills under a different model for verifiers: tool and prompt shapes tuned for one model may degrade on another.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the model itself actually is still obsessed with like cleaning up the output before it sees it
cards.claim: Dex says agents pipe test output through head/tail/grep, miss the failing test, and re-run a five-minute suite repeatedly, burning time and context.
cards.evidence_detail: Example: bun run test into head -n40 then re-run into grep error; he says auto-offloading long output to a file helps but the model's habit persists.
cards.landing: Output backpressure: a wrapper script that runs the suite once, writes full output to a file, and prints only a capped summary plus path.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if it accidentally doesn't do that, then you just ate 5,000 tokens of extra context
cards.claim: Dex argues that relying on the model to remember to filter tool output (jq on gh pr create) is fragile, and that code mode makes output shaping deterministic by logging only the needed field.
cards.evidence_detail: gh pr create example; 5,000-token figure is illustrative. Rhys notes it shows up in code mode as console.log(result.url).
cards.landing: Enforce output limits in scripts rather than in prompt instructions; cap tool output by construction.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex+others
cards.quote: hides a bunch of the intermediate stuff.
cards.claim: Dex endorses chaining tool calls inside one code block so intermediate results never enter context (fetch from A, insert into B, log only the final field), instead of one tool call per hop or a bespoke tool per source/destination pair.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's walk-through; Vaibhav adds that hops become upper-bounded at two model calls instead of N.
cards.landing: Saved workflow scripts that do multi-step gathering (register lookups, CI status, diff stats) and return a short result rather than many tool calls in the main context.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I think bash is going to be considered harmful by the end of 2026.
cards.claim: Dex predicts people will move away from raw bash as the agent execution environment toward code-based execution.
cards.evidence_detail: Prediction made in passing alongside Rhys's list of bash problems (global CLI state, no read-only vs destructive signal, not shareable).
cards.landing: Watch item: shell-script hooks and gates may later be better as typed scripts; no immediate change.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: build these as first class tools... then you pull that in and make it first class
cards.claim: Dex's rule of thumb is to build the very common tools as first-class tools, let users bring MCPs for the long tail, and promote a long-tail tool to first class when it becomes popular so you can context-engineer it.
cards.evidence_detail: Recalled from an earlier whiteboard on MCP versus bash; example is everyone adopting Notion.
cards.landing: Promotion rule for skills/agents/scripts: repeated manual steps become a first-class skill or script once they recur.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you are gonna have to start your context window with 50,000 tokens
cards.claim: Dex notes that listing tools only at the start of a context window makes MCP tool sets static per context and that large tool lists eat context, which tool search tries to offload.
cards.evidence_detail: Paraphrase of his exchange with Vaibhav and Rhys (MCP list-tools at context start; Claude offloads tools to search when there are too many). The 50k figure itself is carded at R29-5.
cards.landing: Keep always-loaded context (CLAUDE.md, skill descriptions, MCP tool lists) small; load detail on demand.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: evaling a CLI for agent friendliness is a really interesting story
cards.claim: Dex flags evaluating a CLI for agent-friendliness as a topic worth an episode, after Vaibhav says BAML measured theirs with a benchmark harness.
cards.evidence_detail: Interest only; no result or number given in this episode.
cards.landing: Idea: measure agent-facing scripts/CLIs (do agents use them correctly first time) before relying on them as backpressure.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: you have to look at the primitives, not the implementation of the primitives
cards.claim: Guest Rhys Sullivan argues for managing a tool catalog (name, input, output) and a good OpenAPI spec rather than betting on bash or code mode, since the format will change; Dex responds 'I like it' and summarises it in his outro.
cards.evidence_detail: Guest's closing takeaways; Dex adopts them in the recap ('schemas and input types').
cards.landing: Keep FixFlow checks and workflows as format-independent scripts with typed inputs and outputs, so they can be re-hosted as skills, hooks or workflows later.

cards.source_title: "Code Mode" Deep Dive (AITW #57)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can basically say like, only give me two levels of depth and everything else, just leave the reference
cards.claim: Dex endorses depth-limited type/schema disclosure, showing two levels and leaving references to fetch on demand, as a token-efficient way to describe tools.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex restating Rhys's implementation; a progressive-disclosure example.
cards.landing: Progressive disclosure for CLAUDE.md: summary at the top, detail behind references loaded only on demand.

gaps: 2026-04-28 No Vibes design docs: Dex is absent (only Vaibhav and Kevin Gregory speak), so no cards; the README episode highlights are Vaibhav's.

Transcripts are auto-captions with no speaker labels beyond names; attribution is by name tag and content. Several statements in the code-mode episode are mainly Rhys Sullivan's, and only those Dex adopts are carded.
The inventory lists AITW #55, #56 and #57 by title only (no URLs) in the 2026-04 and 2026-05 lines; I set in_inventory true on that basis and gave refs as line descriptions, not section letters.
No numbers in these episodes are from experiments; the 1%-per-call compounding and the 50k-token baseline are recalled or illustrative figures.
